**Karadzic arrest hailed as milestone for justice; Serbia faces political fallout**

**BELGRADE, Serbia (CNN)** — The arrest of former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic, one of the world’s most wanted war crimes suspects, drew swift international praise Tuesday and reignited fierce political debate inside Serbia, where he had evaded capture for more than a decade.

Karadzic, indicted by the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague on charges including genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes, was arrested in Serbia after years on the run. He is accused of playing a central role in atrocities committed during the 1992-95 Bosnian war, including the siege of Sarajevo and the 1995 massacre of thousands of Muslim men and boys at Srebrenica.

Serbian officials said the arrest demonstrated Belgrade’s commitment to cooperating with the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, a key condition in Serbia’s efforts to deepen ties with the European Union.

Former U.S. envoy Richard Holbrooke, who brokered the Dayton peace accords that ended the Bosnian war, welcomed the arrest as a long-awaited step toward accountability. Holbrooke has long described Karadzic as one of the principal architects of the Bosnian conflict and said his capture was an important moment for victims and for international justice.

British Foreign Secretary David Miliband also praised the arrest, calling it a significant development for Serbia, Bosnia and the wider region. He said the move showed that those accused of the gravest crimes could not expect to escape justice indefinitely.

The White House welcomed the arrest as well, saying Karadzic should now face trial at The Hague. U.S. officials said the capture underscored the importance of cooperation with international justice mechanisms and marked a positive step for Serbia’s democratic government.

Paddy Ashdown, the former international high representative in Bosnia, said the arrest was “hugely important” for the Balkans and for the survivors of the war. He said bringing Karadzic before the tribunal would help confront the legacy of the conflict and counter the belief that powerful wartime leaders could avoid responsibility.

European Union foreign policy chief Javier Solana called the arrest a major step forward and said it would strengthen Serbia’s relationship with Europe. EU officials have repeatedly said full cooperation with The Hague tribunal is essential for Serbia’s European aspirations.

Serbian Foreign Minister Vuk Jeremic said the operation proved Serbia’s determination to meet its international obligations. He framed the arrest as part of Serbia’s effort to turn toward Europe while upholding the rule of law.

But the move was sharply criticized by Serbian nationalist figures. Aleksandar Vucic, then a leading member of the ultranationalist Serbian Radical Party, condemned the arrest and accused the pro-Western government in Belgrade of betraying Serbian interests. Nationalist supporters of Karadzic have long portrayed him as a wartime defender of Serbs rather than a criminal suspect.

Karadzic had been living under an assumed identity, according to Serbian authorities. His arrest raised immediate questions about how he had avoided capture for so long and whether other fugitives, including former Bosnian Serb military commander Ratko Mladic, might soon be found.

For families of the victims of Srebrenica and Sarajevo, the arrest marked a moment many had waited years to see. Karadzic’s transfer to The Hague was expected to begin the next stage of one of the most high-profile war crimes prosecutions since World War II.

*Belgrade* — Radovan Karadzic, the former Bosnian Serb political leader accused of masterminding some of the worst atrocities in Europe since World War II, has been arrested after more than a decade as one of the world’s most wanted fugitives.

Serbian officials confirmed that Karadzic, who had been sought by the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague, was detained in Serbia after years of evading international justice. His capture marks a major breakthrough in efforts to prosecute those responsible for the 1992–1995 Bosnian war, including the massacre of around 8,000 Muslim men and boys at Srebrenica and the long siege of Sarajevo.

For years, Western diplomats and war crimes prosecutors had portrayed Karadzic as a symbol of impunity in the Balkans. Some officials compared him to “Europe’s Osama bin Laden,” a fugitive whose continued freedom represented both a moral stain and a political obstacle for the region. His arrest is therefore being seen not only as a legal milestone, but also as a turning point in Serbia’s relationship with Europe.

Karadzic had been indicted on charges including genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. He is expected to be transferred to the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, where he will face trial. His wartime military commander, Ratko Mladic, also indicted over Srebrenica and other crimes, remained at large at the time of Karadzic’s arrest.

The detention comes at a crucial moment for Serbia, whose leaders have sought closer ties with the European Union. Brussels has repeatedly made cooperation with the Hague tribunal a key condition for progress toward EU membership. By arresting Karadzic, Serbia’s government has sent a strong signal that it is prepared to meet international demands and break with the nationalist legacy of the 1990s.

European officials welcomed the arrest, saying it could help remove one of the biggest barriers to Serbia’s EU ambitions. The move is likely to strengthen the position of pro-European forces in Belgrade, though it may also provoke anger among hardline nationalists who still view Karadzic as a defender of Serb interests during the Bosnian war.

For survivors of the conflict, the arrest carries deep emotional significance. Many Bosnian Muslims and Croats have long demanded that Karadzic be brought before a court to answer for the mass killings, expulsions and detention camps carried out under Bosnian Serb rule.

After years of false sightings, failed searches and suspicions that he had been protected by sympathetic networks, Karadzic’s capture closes one chapter in the Balkan wars’ unfinished reckoning. It also opens another: a trial expected to revisit the darkest events of the Bosnian conflict and test Serbia’s commitment to a European future.

EU officials described the development as evidence that Belgrade was now prepared to meet its international obligations, and suggested it could improve Serbia’s prospects for eventual European integration. The move was also welcomed in Washington and by officials connected to the tribunal, who said Karadzic’s transfer to The Hague would be essential to completing the unfinished legal reckoning from the Balkan wars.

Holbrooke said no such deal existed, insisting that Karadzic had always remained liable to face justice before the international tribunal.

Paddy Ashdown, the former international high representative in Bosnia and Herzegovina, also praised the arrest, describing it as an important moment for the Balkans and for the credibility of international justice. Ashdown and other international figures argued that Karadzic’s capture sent a message that even senior political leaders accused of mass atrocities could not evade accountability indefinitely.

Serbia’s pro-European government presented the arrest as proof of its seriousness in cooperating with the Hague tribunal. Critics accused the government of surrendering him under Western pressure and claimed the arrest had been staged to please Brussels. Some nationalist leaders described the move as humiliating for Serbia and argued that the government was trading national dignity for progress toward EU membership.

Survivors of the war, especially relatives of victims from Srebrenica and Sarajevo, welcomed the news but stressed that justice would depend on a full trial and conviction. For many, Karadzic’s capture came after years of frustration over his ability to live in hiding while victims’ families continued to seek accountability.

Internationally, the arrest was seen as a breakthrough not only for the Hague tribunal but also for Serbia’s postwar rehabilitation. **CNN — July 22, 2008**

Former Bosnian Serb leader **Radovan Karadzic**, one of the world’s most wanted war crimes suspects, has been arrested in Serbia after more than a decade on the run, Serbian officials said Monday.

Karadzic, who led Bosnian Serbs during the 1992-1995 Bosnian war, was indicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia on charges including **genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes**. The charges stem from atrocities committed during the conflict, including the **1995 massacre at Srebrenica**, where about 8,000 Muslim men and boys were killed, and the prolonged **siege of Sarajevo**.

His capture marks one of the most significant arrests connected to the Balkan wars since the transfer of former Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic to The Hague in 2001.

Karadzic had been a fugitive since 1996, shortly after the signing of the **Dayton Peace Accords**, the U.S.-brokered agreement that ended the Bosnian war and created Bosnia and Herzegovina’s current power-sharing structure between the Bosniak-Croat Federation and Republika Srpska.

Serbian authorities said Karadzic was detained in Belgrade and would be brought before a war crimes court before expected extradition to The Hague. Officials gave few details of the operation, but the arrest was widely viewed as a major test of Serbia’s willingness to cooperate with international justice efforts.

The European Union has repeatedly made cooperation with the U.N. war crimes tribunal a condition for Serbia’s closer ties with the bloc. Western diplomats welcomed the arrest, saying it could improve Belgrade’s prospects for integration with Europe.

“This is an important step for Serbia and for justice in the Balkans,” one European diplomat said. “It demonstrates that cooperation with The Hague is possible and necessary.”

U.S. and European officials praised the move, while emphasizing that other fugitives, including former Bosnian Serb military commander **Ratko Mladic**, remained at large. Mladic has also been indicted in connection with Srebrenica and other wartime atrocities.

Families of victims in Bosnia reacted with relief but caution, saying Karadzic’s arrest came too late for many survivors who had waited years to see him face trial. In Sarajevo, residents described the news as historic, though many said true reconciliation would depend on accountability and acknowledgment of crimes committed during the war.

Karadzic, a former psychiatrist and poet, became the political leader of the Bosnian Serbs as Yugoslavia disintegrated in the early 1990s. Under his leadership, Bosnian Serb forces pursued campaigns that prosecutors have described as ethnic cleansing against Bosniaks and Croats.

His expected transfer to The Hague would place him before the tribunal more than 13 years after the Dayton agreement ended the fighting — and after years of pressure on Serbia to prove it was ready to break with the legacy of the wars that tore apart the former Yugoslavia.
